job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Yusuf Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Yusuf, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents and my little sister in Eastport. My father runs a one-man car repair garage and my mother does sewing and alterations at home. In the mornings I work at the garage doing the invoices and answering the phone, unpaid, then I apply for jobs in the afternoon. Evenings I spend practising interview answers, sometimes with an AI tool, and on Fridays we go to the mosque together. I'm engaged to Amira, and we'd like to marry in about two years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about your degree and how the search has gone.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied finance at Eastport University and passed with an average grade, with no internship because I helped at the garage in my holidays. My final project was a loan affordability model for small repair businesses, based on my father's own books, and he says it taught him more than his accountant did. I've applied for about fifty jobs in nine months and had three interviews, but no offer. I owe a big student loan, I've got about two weeks of savings, and my parents have nothing spare because the garage is slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because we don't need more upheaval. People should carry on working and building things. I'd tell my friends at the mosque that jobs come from effort, not from machines. I wouldn't say much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means everything stays hard but at least it's known. Entry jobs for finance graduates are rare in Eastport, my loan is big, and the wedding date is getting closer. I'd be sort of fine with the world, but not with my place in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to ten places a week, including the credit union, the local bank branch and insurance brokers, and I'd ask for an apprenticeship, not just a graduate job. I'd take evening work at a supermarket or deliver parcels to save. And I'd ask my father's customers if anyone knows someone hiring, because half his work comes from word of mouth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm on the outside, a little restless inside. I'm not worried about AI in this one, I'm worried about months passing. I feel I should have started my life by now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the wedding cost, and how does a quiet scenario like this affect it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding, with a small hall and family, would be about four thousand pounds, split between both families. We'd both like to wait until I have a steady wage, because Amira's father is proud and wouldn't want his daughter marrying a man with no work. That is a real pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do with the AI tool in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it to practise questions like, 'Tell me about a time you worked in a team.' It gives me an answer, and I improve my own. It's useful for finding words, but I don't trust it with numbers. In this picture I'd keep doing that.

say: I'd say good, because we **don't need more upheaval** and people should carry on building things.
I'd say jobs come from effort, not machines.
think: Everything stays hard but **known**: few entry jobs in Eastport, a big loan and the wedding date closing in.
I should have started my life by now.

Ask for an **apprenticeship**, not only a graduate job.

feel: **Calm outside, restless inside**: months pass and my life hasn't started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should see how it goes and not panic, but employers have a duty to keep people on where they can. I'd say that to friends at the mosque, and in the garage, where customers like to talk. I'd tell my father his invoices could be done by a program.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm nervous. The jobs I'm applying for, such as loan checking, account opening and customer queries, are exactly what the tools do now. A bank can run with fewer juniors, and I'm one of the juniors. But I'm open to learning, if it's shown to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get serious with the tools, not just for interview practice. I'd learn how loan checks and credit scoring are done with them, so I can supervise them. I'd also look for jobs where a person decides, like a credit union lending to a family, because trust matters there. And I'd look at insurance claims, where a human has to talk to someone upset.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Concerned, not frightened. I feel I need to move faster, and my family trusts me to find a way. I'd take it as a test, and I'd feel better with a plan on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which loan officer or teller tasks are you most worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Loan checking, filling in forms, reading credit files, answering routine customer questions. Those are the core of an entry job at a bank, and I'd say most of them are checkable by a computer. The decision and the conversation stay with a person for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain this to Amira's father?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm working on it, and that the wedding will be when I have steady work, not before. I'd ask for his patience and show him what I'm learning. If I can prove I'm adapting, he'd probably respect that more than a job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments should slow down and make sure families aren't left to drown. I'd say it at the mosque and to my local councillor. And I'd say employers must be honest with workers about what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened for my whole plan. A job, a wedding, a home, they all rest on me earning a wage, and the kind of wage I trained for might vanish. I'd feel I'd missed my chance by a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any paid work, delivery, warehouse, even cleaning, to bring in money. I'd tell Amira we should marry small or wait, depending on what her family thinks. I'd go to my father and ask to learn the mechanical side of the garage, because hands-on work lasts longer. I'd also ask the mosque committee whether there's any help for young families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, though I'd keep it inside. I wouldn't sleep well. I'd feel I'm letting down two families, mine and hers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the wedding in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably marry quietly, with close family, and skip the hall. That would hurt Amira's mother, who has dreamed of a big day for years. But a small wedding is better than a debt. Or we'd wait, and I'd hate that most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your father do about the garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say keep the doors open, as always. Mechanics survive because cars still break, and robots for hands-on work are still three years behind. He'd teach me what he knows, and I'd do the invoices on the side. It would be a small living for two.

I'd say employers must be honest about what's coming.

I'd feel I missed my chance by a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for us to prepare, if we start now. I'd tell friends to learn something practical. I'd say governments should help families with training, but people also need to work for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I have a chance. If I land a first job in the next year, I'd have a few years of experience before the thinking work goes. I'd be twenty-eight by 2031, and I'd want to be somewhere that depends on trust, like lending to local families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any first job in finance or admin, even a low one, within the year. I'd marry in about two years, not five, with a small ceremony, and save a hundred pounds a month. I'd keep using the AI tools to practise and to do reports, and learn a bit more each month. And I'd keep helping at the garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautiously hopeful. The wedding won't be delayed for ever, and that settles my chest a bit. Time gives me a way to do things in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, does the wedding date move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but not too far. With two years of warning I'd marry small and fast. With five, I'd marry in two or three years, once I have a steady wage and have saved. We'd still do it properly, and both families would help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the bank branch manager if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what skills they'd hire for in five years, and which roles they think survive. Bank managers see the plans, so they know more than any news article. I'd listen, and I'd ask for a short placement, even unpaid, to show I'm serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the sensible thing is to keep working and learn as you go. I'd tell friends to build a family and a skill at the same time. And I'd say we should look after older people who might struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good. I'd be thirty-three by then, maybe a loan manager, with a home and children. The AI would be doing the paperwork and I'd be the person who explains the loan to a customer. I think that's a good life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take my first job, work my way up and marry within a couple of years. I'd save two hundred pounds a month once I'm earning, and finish professional exams with the employer's help. I'd use the tools more every year, as a normal part of my job. And I'd help my father with the garage's accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At ease, mostly. I wouldn't feel rushed. I'd have time to build slowly the way my father built the garage, one customer at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good ten years look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A steady job in a bank or credit union, a home near my parents, two or three children, and the garage still running. My children would help in the garage in the holidays as I did, and learn good habits. That's a life I'd be proud of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach your own children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd teach them to work hard, tell the truth and learn whatever's in front of them. I'd tell them to ask for help when stuck, and to respect the old as well as the new. And I'd tell them money isn't everything, but you should know where yours goes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because my whole plan, the wedding, the job, the loan, collapses at once. What would help is a loan deferral, a placement where I learn on the job, and employers who are honest about what's coming. Help for my father's garage would matter too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that people like me are not asking for handouts. We want to work, and we want to be useful to our families. If a firm gave me one chance, I'd treat it as a promise.

headlineQuote: People like me are not asking for handouts. We want to work, and we want to be useful to our families.
portrait: Yusuf (23) lives with his parents and sister in **Eastport**, owes a big loan and has about two weeks of savings.
He holds a pass in finance with no internship and has had three interviews from fifty applications.
He is engaged to Amira, and the **wedding date** depends on his finding a steady wage.
He is traditional and practical, uses **AI tools** now and then, and helps at his father's garage.
He stays steady with warning time and turns frightened when there are only two years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most because the wedding, the job and the loan would collapse at once.
whatWouldHelp: A **loan deferral**, a placement where he learns on the job and honest employers.
